column1: Original
Game Overview
After registration you start on a tiny planet in one of the many star systems in the galaxy.
You begin by building up your planet, then you can colonize uninhabited planets expanding your empire.
Once you think your fleet is strong enough, you can engage in battles with other players and take over their planets!
You'll need to plan carefully and use diplomacy to help you in order to succeed in this competition with thousands of players from all over the world!
Game Objective
Expansion of your own space empire and/or the supremacy of your own alliance by means of war, diplomacy and planet development.
As you colonize further planets, your total points will increase and your level of development and ranking will improve.
The winner is the first player to reach or exceed 500 points for a total of seven days, or the first alliance to reach or exceed 360 points for a total of three days. See Countdown for more details.
System Requirements
Astro Wars runs in real-time and is web-based, so you can play from anywhere with no installation, as long as you have a web browser and an internet connection.
The game also has a WAP interface. Rounds can last for up to three months.

Alliance Ranking & Points

The Alliance Points represent the average score of the top members within the alliance — not everyone counts equally.

    All players in the alliance are sorted by their ranking points (from highest to lowest).
    The game decides how many players should count for the alliance score. It uses this rule:
    - CountingMembers = totalPlayers - (totalPlayers / 4)
    - But at least 3 players always count, even in small alliances.
    The points of those top players are added together and divided by the number of counted players to get the final alliance score.

Formula:
Alliance Points = (Sum of Top Counting Members) ÷ Counting Members (rounded down)

Example:
An alliance has 8 members with the following points:
116, 111, 92, 85, 80, 52, 46, 40

Top 6 counting players → 116 + 111 + 92 + 85 + 80 + 52 = 536
Average → 536 ÷ 6 = 89,3
Rounded down → 89 Alliance Points

Once a player has founded an alliance he has first right to use the alliance tag in the next round, he also will not need to pay the founder's fee again. The founder will display the reserved tag from the beginning of the round, but he will not have any benefits of the alliance or the use of the alliance screen until he has achieved Player Level 1. If you launch a fleet to an alliance member's planet you get 50% speed bonus, as if you had launched to your own planet. You can also access the Alliance Screen where you can see details about other members, such as planets owned (system ID and planet ID, with their order) and their infrastructure, production/science/culture per hour, incoming fleet alerts, idle times, race, fleet locations (with arrival time if launched), trade revenue and partners, science and culture levels.
Trade Agreement

A Trade Agreement (TA) can be made between two Players. For twenty thousand Astro Dollars you can send or accept an offer of a Trade Agreement to or with another player. Every Player may have a maximum of 5 Trade Agreements with different partners. The Update for Trade Agreements occurs only once each day.

If the other player accepts (costing him/her 20000 Astro Dollars as well, except for the Trader Race). Then you will get an income bonus (Production Points (PP), Science (SP), Culture/hour, Growth/hour). You will receive 1% for each planet your trade partners own which have a population equal to or greater than 10.

Example: you have two trade partners. Partner A has five planets with populations of 15, 14, 5, 5, 3 and partner B has four planets with populations of 11, 10, 10, 2. You will receive 2% from partner A and 3% from partner B, so your total Trade Revenue will be equal to 5%.
Trade Agreement Screen

The total bonus received from Trade Agreements will be shown in the Trade Screen, listed as Trade Revenue, and changes in accordance with your partners' population levels increasing (or decreasing due to resignation/loss of planet).
There are three levels of status for a Trade Agreement:
1. request is pending = the player has made an offer, but the player he offered it to has not yet accepted it;
2. establishing trade infrastructure = the offer was accepted and will be activated at the next Daily Update;
3. active trading = the agreement is activated and the player receives the bonus next to that partner's name.

Note: The player only receives bonuses from 'active trading' agreements, but the number of agreement slots used out of the limit of five includes all accepted offers, which means those marked 'establishing trade infrastructure' as well as those which are 'active trading'.

Example: In the above image, 'active trading' shows the player earns 18% from Oin; 'establishing trade infrastructure' indicates the offer received from crogy has been accepted by the player and will become active at the next Daily Update; 'request is pending' indicates the player offered a Trade Agreement to Brittany who has not yet accepted it. The number of agreement slots used is 2/5 - Oin and crogy, because one is active and one is accepted and waiting to become active.
Trade Revenue
The Trade Revenue is the bonus you get in Growth, Production, Science and Culture per hour. You get bonus for Trade Agreements and the Economy science.
Notes
You are not able to cancel a Trade Agreement once you accepted the offer or your offer was accepted.
If your offer is declined, the agreement is cancelled and your money will be returned almost immediately.
If your offer is not responded to within after 48 hours, it is cancelled and your money is returned.

Upon mutual acceptance of a Trade Agreement you will not receive the bonuses until after the next Daily Update at 03:00 GMT (02:00 GMT during daylight saving). Until this time, the status will show as 'establishing trade infrastructure'.

column1: Production Points

Production Points (PP) are needed to build fleet and enhance the buildings on your planets. Each planet receives 1PP/hour for each level of Robotic Factory built on it, and all planets gain 1PP/hour for each level of Population. Production Points earned are calculated on a decimal basis.

When all your planets attain a combined total greater than 150 PP, you have the option to "Spend All Points". You can use this to sell all your PP for Astro Dollars (even from sieged planets, although only 70% of the PP from a sieged planet goes to you, with the remaining 30% being lost). Alternatively you can choose to spend them all on a war ship or Starbase.

column1: Using Spend All will not gather up all of your PP then let you choose one planet to spend them on. This option spends the PP at each planet in turn on the option you selected, according to the amount of PP found there. So this is not a way to move production points between planets (you should use Colony Ships for that), it is a way of buying the same item on each of your planets in a single transaction.

Example: if you have 60 PP on Planet 1; 25 on Planet 2; 65 on Planet 3 you would have enough cumulative points for exactly 5 Destroyers (assuming a cost of 30 PP each). However you will actually get 2 Destroyers on Planet 1, 83% of a Destroyer on Planet 2, and 2 Destroyers plus 66% of another one on Planet 3, giving you an actual total of 4 complete Destroyers, and some points towards others on two of the three planets.

To sell all of your PP for Astro Dollars you must choose the "Interstellar Trade" option on the Spend All screen. The effect of selling PP is immediate, you do not need to wait until the Daily Update to earn and use the money.

column1: Supply Units
For each new Player Level you reach, you will earn a supply unit. Your maximum supply unit capacity is also equal to your current Player Level.
Spending Supply Units

To spend supply units on buildings, just click on the appropriate button on the lower part of the Spend Points Menu in your Planets Screen. This lower part only shows when you actually own supply units, and will also show any partial refund you may receive for buying certain buildings.
Supply Unit strategy
Most players spend their supply units on Robotic Factories or Galactic Cybernets to directly increase their production or culture, for a faster development.

Spending supply units on Hydroponic Farms on all of your planets can dramatically increase your population (providing you have a sufficient Social science level), and your score by the same amount. It can be up to two times cheaper than using them on Robotic Factories. You can also spend them all on a single planet to make it your new capital (since planets are sorted by population).

Spending supply units on Research Labs is the most cost-effective short term choice, especially if you started with a level 12 Research Lab. It can be handy when the supply unit's price is too unstable, or if you just need to boost your science.
If you notice a significant change in the supply unit price's variation amplitude (or for anything else you can buy or sell!), you can try "playing the market". This is how to do it:
Buy when the price is low
Sell when the price is high

In the late stages of each round, the supply unit's price tends to witness some kind of "resonance" and keeps going up and down. It is due to naïve players who think they can earn money using this method, causing big changes in demand or supply, and therefore the price.
Notes
Supply Units can be spent on any building except Starbases to increase its level.
You can also buy additional supply units from the Trade menu.
You can also sell supply units for Astro Dollars from the Trade Screen.
Planets

Planets are the basis for development and battle in Astro Wars. Each member of the game is spawned on a single planet, named after the Star System it's located in, called the Planet ID. Some planets are created without an owner (Free) and many are controlled by Unknown. Players control their planets from the Planets Screen, managing the various buildings. The number of possible owned planets directly relates to the player's Culture level.
Unknown Owner

If you see a planet to be owned by Unknown, this just means that its former owner has resigned. The unknown player has a neutral race and an overall science level of zero (thus giving you a fighting bonus). If a player becomes unknown, remaining fleet on his planets does not disappear. However, any fleet in transit disappears. This applies to Transports and Colony Ships as well, though they pose no threat to attacking fleets.

column1: Unknown planets do not continue to generate Production Points after abandonment, but you do get is 10% of the Production Points from the former owner, up to a maximum of 500pp. Therefore, unknown planets are often preferred targets for colonization as opposed to Free Planets, since they offer players extra PPs and existing buildings.
Some say that artifacts might be found on the unknown planets. However, this does not happen very often.
Colonizing A Free Planet

You can colonize unowned planets (Free) with a Colony Ship if your Culture level is higher than your total number of planets. Firstly, you will need to build a Colony Ship by spending production points on any one of your planets. After that, you can launch it via the Fleet Screen towards the selected target.

Generally, it is wise to send an escort with the Colony Ship, to ensure its safety. If the planet is under siege by another player at the time of arrival (marked red in the Star System Detail Screen), you will need an escorting war fleet strong enough to defeat the sieging ships in battle, or your ships will be destroyed.
Conquering an Owned or Unknown Planet

In order to expand your empire, you will inevitably have to Conquer someone else's planet at some point. Whilst taking some Building Damage, the buildings are at least partially saved. You will find 10% of the production points that were on the planet before you colonized it, up to a maximum of 500 Production Points. To conquer a planet, you must have a Fleet capable of destroying any Starbase and/or Defending Fleet the player might have there, plus Transports at least equal in quantity to the Population (1 Transport can destroy 1 Population). When the Population reaches 0, control of the planet is turned over to the attacker (assuming the attacker has a high enough level of Culture to sustain another planet).

Example: if a Planet has a Population of 6, defended by 2 Destroyers and a Starbase level 4, an attacker would need at least 6 Transports, and a fleet worth 45 CV (in any combination of Destroyers, Cruisers and Battleships) to win.
Notes

If your culture level increases after your fleet arrives, you will need to re-launch the transports so they arrive again. To avoid this, use the Arrival Time Calculator to help schedule your arrival for a little later than your increase in culture, so you have sufficient time to log in.

column1: ETA Calculator

This is part of the Fleet Screen and allows you to check the estimated time of arrival (ETA) of a fleet before launching your fleet. The calculator is available to all players, and is very accurate to within one or two seconds. Fleet arrivals are processed by the game server in the strict sequence the launch command is received, so if two fleets have the same arrival time, the one which is launched first will always arrive first.

Using this feature will help you to tactically calculate the best time to lunch an attack, to catch your opponent off-guard and minimize his/her reaction or preparation time. Be aware, that even though estimations are quite precise, the fleet will be shown as "pending" on arrival for up to one minute until the fleet screen refreshes.
Notes
You can only have a maximum of 5 fleets in transit at any given time.

Combat value (CV) refers to how well a ship or starbase will fair in a battle.
Each of the three war ships has a Combat Value based on its attack and defense properties. A Starbase Combat value is based solely on its defense.
To calculate the combat Value of each ship, simply add the Attack Value and Defense Value together. To calculate the Combat value of a fleet, combine the combat value of all ships in the Fleet.
Example
A Fleet consisting of 10 Destroyers, 2 Cruisers and 10 Battleships would have a combat value of 678:

It is most probable, but not always true, that a fleet with a higher CV than an opposing Fleet, or defensive Starbase will win the Battle, however, there are possibilities that it may not, luck and odds are a factor in every close battle.
To properly calculate the possible outcome of a battle, use the Battle Calculator.
Defense value
The higher the Defense Value of a ship is, the higher the chance that it will survive a battle.

When predicting the outcome of a battle, Defense Value of a fleet should be combined with Attack Value to give the Combat Value (CV). The Starbase's Defense Value should be added to both Attack Value and Defense Value of the defending fleet to provide a relatively reliable prediction of the outcome of the battle (assuming both sides have equal scientific levels of Physics and Mathematics).
Notes
The owner of the defending planet will always get a warning of the incoming fleet detailing the offensive ships and how many transports are incoming with an ETA (See: Arrival Time Calculator).

Non Aggression Pact

A Non Aggression Pact (also known as "NAP") is an agreement between players or alliances not to attack each other. Nothing more, nothing less. Should include some termination clause, if you care about your reputation and want to avoid Backstabbing.
Friendly Fleets

Friendly fleet is the term used to describe the fleet of an ally or NAP partner. Usually friendly fleets are sent to a planet to use it as a jump point close to an enemy to attack with very little warning, or to defend the planet from attack.

An alliance member will know when his fleet is being sent to a friendly planet, as the launch will be cancelled and an alert will appear in the Fleet Screen, warning that a Non Aggression Pact has been detected.
Friendly Attack
Friendly Attack (FA) or Friendly Fire (FF) is a tactic used to boost Player Levels and earn Supply Units early in the game.
Friendly Siege

This is when a player sieges an ally's planet allowing them to control where the sieged player's production points will go when buying production points, as they are always allocated to the first unsieged planet listed in the Planets Screen.

This allows the sieged player to quickly develop weak planets far down the list, or to build urgently needed forces ready for either rapid defence on that planet (probably starbases), or to go to a planet which is closer to here for purposes of rapid defence or attack.

Race
After your first login you see the page on the right:

The first link will use the default race, the other one gives the option to modify your Race to take bonuses or maluses in your attributes. This will give advantages and disadvantages in certain areas of the game.
Creating a Race

When creating a race, a player can choose to change his/her attributes positively or negatively. All players start with an attribute offset equal to zero. Players can decide then to increase one attribute, but must choose another to decrease in order to maintain an offset equal to zero. For example, the ability to study science can be increased by 16%, which will result in an offset of -2, and this offset must then be reduced to zero by choosing a decrease in another attribute, for example Growth by -14%. You can see the percentage changes and the related offsets while setting your own race.
Race Options
The attributes that can be increased or decreased are:
Growth: how fast your Population will grow
Science: how fast Research of Science is
Culture: how soon you can colonize new planets
Production: affects Production Point output on all planets
Speed: how fast Fleets travel between Planets and Star Systems
Attack: affects Attack Value
Defense: affects Defense Value
Player Level growth also depends on Race. Each level above the default (+0) setting for Speed, Attack and Defense will give 0.1% increase per day.
Players also have the option to choose a:
Trader Race: Ability to accept Trade Agreements for free;
Research Lab 12 for their first planet.
Notes

Whichever choices are made, the offset value must always be equal to zero. This means that any increases in one or more attributes must be balanced by decreases in others to the same cumulative value.
The default race (no race) gives 0% bonus in Growth, Production, Science, Speed, Attack, Defense and the subsequent default Player Level increases spontaneously by 1.2% per day at the Daily Update.
General Info
Help! I'm lost?

So you want to play AstroWars? This guide is an introduction to the basics of the game, to help you survive the first days and understand how things work. You will see many words in gold, these are links to other pages offering more detail about that topic.
Game Interface

There are seven main screens in the interface, accessed from tabs located along the top of the page. These also lead to other screens used to perform specific tasks within each activity type. Collectively these make up your Control Panel.
News screen

When you log in, this is the first page you see. It shows your news alerts for the last seven days, presented five to each page, covering every activity which affects your game. For details of how this screen works, see the News Screen page.
Map screen

This displays all the star systems within your range of travel. Here you can view details of the owner, population and starbase level for all planets in each system shown. For details of how this screen works, see the Map Screen page.
Planet screen

This is where you manage your planets, and spend Production Points on buildings and ships. At the start of the game you should first buy Robotic Factory, to generate more production points at a faster rate. For more help, see Planets Screen.
Science screen

This screen manages your Research Lab. Research is important as it can give you better ships, more planets etc. You can only research one science at a time, but can change your selection at any time. For more help, see the Science Screen.
Trade screen

Once you reach player level 1 you can use this page to buy and sell Artifacts, Supply Units, and Production Points. You can also make Trade Agreements with other players to earn bonuses. For more details, see the main Trade Screen help.
Alliance screen

If you gain a certain level of dollars and Player Level 1, this appears in the interface. If you are an alliance member, this shows the development and activity of all your allies. More details on this can be found on the Alliance Screen page.
Fleet screen

Here you can control your fleet and launch attacks on other players. The screen shows the quantity and location of each ship type you own, and lists all your launched fleets with their arrival times. For more details, see the Fleet Screen page.
Basic Activities
Planets

You start the game with a planet. Each hour you can gain points which accumulate over time to increase your Production, Population, Science and Culture. To earn more points each hour you can build four types of Buildings: Hydroponic Farm, Robotic Factory, Galactic Cybernet and Research Lab. Each one helps you improve a different area of your development.
Sciences

As you increase your planet's buildings and production, you will also want to increase your science. Sciences are used to develop stronger fleets and defenses, see more of the map, and increase your Culture so you can colonize more planets.
Map

If you click on Map and after that on the Star in the middle you can see your direct neighbors who share your Starsystem with you. By clicking on their names you can see details about them and how to contact them.
Sending fleets

As well as increasing your buildings, you can use your production points to buy ships to attack other players. Each war ship type has a different level of weapons and armor, but at the beginning you can only use Destroyers.
Daily updates

Various updates are applied to the game and your development each day. Updates to production points and new levels of development occur every fifteen minutes; scheduled game updates take place at 11:00 GMT, 23:00 GMT and 03:00 GMT.

Advanced Help
Building up

As you earn production points, you can spend them on all your buildings or concentrate on a single building to increase its level. The higher level a building reaches, the more points it will produce each hour. Each building affects a different area of your development, but each level costs more to reach:
Hydroponic Farm will increase your rate of population growth;
Robotic Factory will increase your rate of production points;
Galactic Cybernet will increase the rate of culture development;
Research Lab will increase your rate of science development;
Starbase will increase your level of planetary defenses.

Using a race

If you want to, you can make a race when you first log in to the game at the start of the round. Creating a race allows you to choose your strengths and weaknesses by taking bonuses or maluses in specific areas of your development.

You might choose to become a Trader or start with a level 12 Research Lab, or perhaps you wish to take a bonus in some area of your development. The areas you can choose are: Growth, Science, Culture, Production, Speed, Attack, Defense. Note: This is a very advanced feature intended for experienced players, as getting it wrong can spoil your game.

Expansion
There are three ways of building up your empire, described below:
Pacifism

This is the passive method, achieved by sending messages to all the players in your system offering them non-aggression pacts. You then only take over planets that are unclaimed (Free Planet), or have been abandoned (unknown), or that are owned by inactive players (still showing population level of 1 after a week of game play, or only 1 or 2 logins per day). The objective is to build an empire without antagonizing others as a means of self-preservation.
Hostility

This is the aggressive approach, by which you try to take over the planets of other players in your system as quickly as possible. As the strategy requires skill, timing and a good understanding of the races and attributes of others, it is not recommended for inexperienced or new players. The objective is to be aggressive, not seeking friends or alliances, caring only for the expansion of personal empire.
Alliance

The third and most popular method is a mixture of the first two. This is achieved by registering an alliance with *some* of the players around you, then taking over the ones who are weakest. The objective is to pursue the principle of survival of the fittest by working with those who are strong, to build an empire collectively.
Diplomacy
Diplomacy is the key to success in this game, and there are three types of basic diplomacy:
Alliance

Everything you do is for the alliance, if they are stronger it makes you stronger. You protect them, help out in need, just as the other members of your alliance do for you. To be able to win the round an alliance must have 5 or more members.
NAP

With a NAP (Non Aggression Pact), you only mutually agree with other players and/or alliances not to destroy each other. Often it is a detailed written agreement, with sections covering the sharing of systems, how to end the NAP, relations with each other's friends and allies, aiding the enemies of the other NAP partners, etc.
Coalition

This falls between the other two. Coalition members exchange destroyers in friendly fire to increase Player Level, have a NAP, share information about battle plans, enemy races and locations, execute joint operations against common enemies.
Research Lab
Research Labs house state-of-the-art computer equipment, creating a superior research environment which increases your science output by one(1) each level.
This increase in science output allows for greater levels of science to be reached in less time.
A highly important building for the more scientific rulers.
Galactic Cybernet
Galactic Cybernets are important for interplanetary communications and management, and each new Galactic Cybernet will provide +1 Culture per hour.
Culture will increase faster with more Galactic Cybernets; therefore, your maximum number of planets will increase faster with more Galactic Cybernets, since you will be able to colonize sooner.

Robotic factories increase the production output of a planet by one extra Production Point an hour per level.

Once level 20 is reached, it may appear Robotic Factories cannot be upgraded further, as "N/A" appears in the PP to next level column. This is not so, all buildings (Starbases included) are always upgradeable, due to the formula used to calculate the output levels ratio. Buildings
There are five kinds of buildings, as described below. The development of a building will improve its level, which in turn increases the benefit it provides.

Hydroponic Farm - increases your population growth. Each level adds +1 to the population's rate of growth/hour (that rate is the + figure next to the word "Population" at the top of the Planets Screen);
Robotic Factory - increases production growth. Each level adds +1 to a planet's production/hour, which increases the rate at which a player gains points to spend;

Galactic Cybernet - increases culture growth. Each level adds +1 to the rate/hour by which culture grows in the Science Screen. Culture level is the maximum number of planets a player can own at any one time;
Research Lab - increases science growth. Each level adds +1 to the rate of science research/hour at the top of the Science Screen;
Starbase - increases the planet's static defence. Each level raises the defence value of the starbase, making it more difficult to destroy.

Description
A player’s level is displayed in whole numbers (Actual Level) and a percentage (% to next level).

Example: Player level 9 – 62% would mean the player is 62% of the way to player level 10. Be careful, the formula is not linear, but exponential. You have actually less experience points (XP) than the XP for PL9 + 62% of the XP for PL10. You can find your real number of experience points using a tool, or the following formula :
XP = 5 x (pl)^2,7 - 5 x (pl-1)^2,7; with a decimal value for PL (9.62 in the example)
The PL value shown in the profile is always rounded down. (1.999 is shown as 1-99%).
